title: Why Hasidim Dress This Way
hookLine: Hasidic dress keeps the memory of old Eastern Europe
carry: dress that remembers, dress to meet god
tomorrow: The Niggun: A Song Without Words

cards: A closet holds a story if you know how to read it. A wedding dress in a garment bag. A grandfather's watch in a drawer.

A jersey that only comes out on game day. On a Friday afternoon in a Hasidic neighborhood, the men come out in long black silk coats, and some wear round fur hats, wide and tall, that look like nothing else on the street.
To a passerby it looks like a costume. To the people wearing it, it's closer to that watch in the drawer.

teach.b: Clothes remember. First, the pieces. The long coat, called a bekishe or a kapote.
The fur hat on Shabbat, a shtreimel, or in some courts a taller one, a spodik. A belt, the gartel, tied around the waist for prayer. Each court has its own details, down to the shape of a hat.
Second, the memory. Tradition says this is, broadly, how Jewish men and nobles in parts of Eastern Europe once dressed.
The world around them changed its clothes. The Hasidim kept theirs. So the coat says: we have not forgotten where we come from.
A midrash some Hasidim quote says that in Egypt the Israelites held on to their own names and their own language, and some versions add their own dress. Third, dressing for God.
The Talmud tells of a sage who would put on fine shoes before praying, citing the prophet Amos: "prepare to meet thy God, O Israel."
Hasidim speak of the gartel in the same spirit, a line drawn around the body before standing to pray. Fourth, what it isn't. The clothes are not the faith, and Hasidim themselves don't say they are.
Other Jews dress in all kinds of ways and pray just as seriously.
But cloth can hold a memory the way a melody can.
Look back over this week: two souls, always joyful, you can repair, truth, fiercely, hidden will, named for towns. And today, a coat that remembers.

how: In Hasidic courts, men wear a long dark coat and tie a gartel for prayer, and on Shabbat and festivals married men in some courts put on a fur shtreimel or spodik; the details differ from court to court.

games.q: the world around them changed its clothes. the Hasidim had to choose. what did they do?
o: kept the old Eastern European dress.
games.why: they kept theirs, and the coat became a way of saying: we have not forgotten where we come from.

practice: Look down at what you're wearing right now and pick one thing: a ring, a scarf, a pair of shoes. Ask where it came from, who gave it, where you bought it, what you were doing the first time you wore it, and let the memory come up.
Then picture one thing you might put on for a reason you can name: to honor someone, or to get ready for something that matters.

wordCard.voice: Clothes remember. Hasidic dress, the long coat, the fur hat, the prayer belt, keeps the memory of old Eastern Europe and turns getting dressed into getting ready. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a garment, a piece of clothing.

carryVoice: Your line: dress that remembers, dress to meet God. The coat keeps a memory; the gartel gets you ready to pray. Until tomorrow.
